f.t: The Akimel O’otham welcomed the Pee Posh (Maricopa) to the Gila River long ago, and the two peoples still share its lands and resources today.
Akimel O’otham basket weaving is in revival, and in 2004 the community dedicated the Huhugam Heritage Center to care for its heritage.
In 1859 Congress created the first reservation in Arizona along the Gila River, in appreciation of the Akimel O’otham role in westward travel.

n.l: Gila River Indian Community, south of Phoenix, Arizona, US, shared with the Pee Posh (Maricopa)

f.t: The Pueblo of Zuni counts about 18,692 people and holds about 463,287 acres of reservation land.
For about the last 300 years most Zuni people have lived in one main village, the Pueblo of Zuni, with farming villages used at planting and harvest.

n.l: Pueblo of Zuni along the Zuni River in western New Mexico, US, with reservation land in Arizona

f.t: The Chiricahua Apache Nation describes its governance through an Executive Council and National Council made up of citizen-descendants.
The Chiricahua Apache Nation lists its tribal headquarters in Santa Clara, New Mexico.
Its foundation's stated work includes education, social welfare and defending Chiricahua Apache self-determination.

n.l: Headquarters in Santa Clara, New Mexico, United States; this record describes this named community, not every Chiricahua Apache person or government

f.t: About 1,000 Cocopah tribal members live and work on or near their reservation south of Yuma, Arizona, which was established in 1917.

f.p: Sistema de Información Cultural, Secretaría de Cultura (Mexico)
f.t: Since 2003 the Cucapá of El Mayor, Baja California, and the Cocopah of Somerton, Arizona, have met each year with dances, songs, crafts and food.
The Cocopah, known as the River People, have lived along the lower Colorado River and its delta for centuries.

n.l: Lower Colorado River and delta: south of Yuma and near Somerton, Arizona, US, and the Mexicali valley of Baja California and San Luis Río Colorado, Sonora, Mexico

f.p: Sistema de Información Cultural, Secretaría de Cultura (Mexico)
f.t: In 1975 Mexico declared the Canal del Infiernillo an exclusive Comcaac fishing zone and symbolically granted them Tiburón Island, a nature reserve, as communal land.

f.p: Sistema de Información Cultural, Secretaría de Cultura (Mexico)
f.t: Comcaac artisans weave coritas, baskets made since before Spanish contact. A very large one can take a year or two to finish.

n.l: Desert coast of Sonora on the Gulf of California, Mexico, including Punta Chueca, El Desemboque and Tiburón Island

f.t: Diné Bikéyah, the Navajo Nation, covers more than 27,000 square miles across Arizona, New Mexico and Utah, larger than 10 of the 50 US states.
The Navajo Nation Council, the Nation’s governing body, has 24 delegates elected from legislative districts.
In World War II, Navajo Code Talkers used the Navajo language to create a military code that was never broken by the enemy.

n.l: Diné Bikéyah (Navajoland) across Arizona, New Mexico and Utah, US

f.t: Since 2017 the Acoma Language Program has been building a Keres dictionary, with about 5,000 words and phrases being edited by fluent speakers.
In 1999 Acoma set up a Historic Preservation Office to keep traditional skills alive, among them stone cutting, wood carving, pottery making and weaving.
Archaeologists agree that Acoma has been lived in continuously since at least AD 1200, and Acoma oral history reaches back much further.

n.l: Acoma Mesa and surrounding lands in west-central New Mexico, US

f.t: Supai is so remote that the US Postal Service carries all mail in and out of the canyon by mule train.
The Havasupai reservation was set up in 1880 and greatly enlarged in 1975. It covers 188,077 acres beside the South Rim of the Grand Canyon.
The Havasu Baaja, People of the Blue Green Waters, have made the village of Supai below the Grand Canyon rim their home for over 1,000 years.

n.l: Havasu Canyon in the Grand Canyon, Arizona, US (village of Supai)

f.t: The Hopi Reservation in northeastern Arizona covers more than 1.5 million acres and is made up of 12 villages on three mesas.
Hopi government is unicameral. Its powers rest with a Tribal Council of village representatives, who serve two year terms.
Hopi farmers developed dry farming, using windbreaks to hold soil, snow and moisture so corn, beans and squash can grow in a dry land.

n.l: Hopitutskwa, northeastern Arizona, US (Navajo and Coconino counties)

f.t: Hualapai River Runners is the only Indian-owned and operated river rafting company on the Colorado River.
The Hualapai Reservation, set up in 1883, covers about one million acres along 108 miles of the Grand Canyon and Colorado River.
The name Hualapai means People of the Tall Pines.

n.l: Northwestern Arizona, US, along the Grand Canyon and Colorado River (Peach Springs)

f.t: The Jicarilla Apache Nation reservation spans more than 879,917 acres in north-central New Mexico, and Dulce is its only community and tribal headquarters.
Jicarilla elders still read the coming spring flows and summer water supply from the timing of snowfall, knowledge that closely tracks what scientists call moisture content.
After 1887 the Jicarilla moved their individual allotments back into tribal ownership, keeping their lands and water rights together.

n.l: North-central New Mexico, US, along the Colorado line and across the Continental Divide (Dulce)

f.t: People of Santa Clara Pueblo still speak the Tewa language today and carry on their customs and cultural activities.
Santa Clara is one of six Tewa-speaking villages, and its reservation covers about 90 square miles from the Jemez Mountains to the Rio Grande.
Santa Clara offers guided tours of Puje, its ancestral village about 10 miles from the present pueblo, to share how the ancestors lived.

n.l: From the eastern Jemez Mountains to the Rio Grande, northern New Mexico, US

f.p: Sycuan Band of the Kumeyaay Nation
f.t: North of the US and Mexico border there are 12 Kumeyaay Nation bands today, each original to Kumeyaay territory. Sycuan is one of them.

f.p: Sistema de Información Cultural, Secretaría de Cultura (Mexico)
f.t: In Baja California the Kumiai call themselves Tipai. Their communities sit on the coastal plateaus of Ensenada and Rosarito and in Tecate.

f.p: Sistema de Información Cultural, Secretaría de Cultura (Mexico)
f.t: Kumiai weavers make baskets from willow branches, called shikwines, and from rush, called sawiles, knowing the right season to cut each material.

n.l: San Diego and Imperial counties, California, US, and Tecate, Ensenada and Rosarito in Baja California, Mexico

f.t: In 2021, the City and County of Presidio donated a Lipan cemetery parcel to the Lipan Apache Tribe.
The Tribe recounts that by 1880, Lipan communities lived along the Rio Grande on both sides of the United States-Mexico border.
The Lipan Apache Tribe in Texas maintains a Tribal Council responsible for community welfare and protection of its heritage.

n.l: Texas, United States, with tribal administration in McAllen and historical homelands spanning Texas and northern Mexico

f.t: Today three peoples, the Mescalero, Lipan and Chiricahua Apache, together make up the Mescalero Apache Tribe on a 463,000 acre reservation.
The Mescalero Apache Tribe owns and runs the Inn of the Mountain Gods Resort and the Ski Apache ski area.
The Tribe is governed by an eight member Tribal Council with an elected President and Vice-President, each chosen by secret ballot for two years.
Chiricahua Apache families arrived at the Mescalero reservation in 1913 after imprisonment at Fort Sill, Oklahoma.

n.l: South-central New Mexico, US (Mescalero Apache Reservation)

f.t: The Ute Mountain Ute Tribe teaches the Ute language to Head Start children ages 2 to 5 and holds evening language classes for adults.
There are three Ute tribes today: the Southern Ute (Mouache and Capote bands), the Ute Mountain Ute (Weenuche band) and the Northern Ute in Utah.

n.l: Southwestern Colorado (Ignacio, Towaoc), northeastern Utah (Uintah and Ouray) and nearby New Mexico and Utah lands, US

f.t: Ohkay Owingeh is the headquarters of the Eight Northern Pueblo Tribal Council.
The people have long called their home Ohkay Owingeh, place of the strong people in Tewa, and officially restored that name in place of San Juan, given in 1598.
People have lived at Ohkay Owingeh since about AD 1200, farming with irrigation along the Rio Grande.

n.l: Where the Rio Grande and Rio Chama meet, northern New Mexico, US

f.p: Sistema de Información Cultural, Secretaría de Cultura (Mexico)
f.t: Rarámuri artisans make violins, drums, palm baskets, clay pots and wooden masks, and sell them in towns such as Guachochi, Creel and Batopilas.

f.p: Sistema de Información Cultural, Secretaría de Cultura (Mexico)
f.t: The Rarámuri ball race is a contest in which runners cover long distances while kicking a wooden ball, and it is held as part of community fiestas.

f.p: Sistema de Información Cultural, Secretaría de Cultura (Mexico)
f.t: From the 1700s to today the Rarámuri have practiced a quiet resistance, and some moved to remote parts of the sierra to keep their traditions.

n.l: Sierra Tarahumara in Chihuahua, Mexico, with smaller communities in Durango, Sonora and Sinaloa

f.t: The San Carlos Apache Reservation, set aside in 1871, covers 1,834,781 acres reaching from alpine meadows to desert in southeastern Arizona.
More than a third of San Carlos land is forest or woodland, giving a home to elk, mule deer, black bear, turkeys and mountain lion.
The San Carlos Apache Tribe opened its first Cultural Center in Peridot in 1995 so its people could tell their own story.

n.l: Gila, Graham and Pinal counties, southeastern Arizona, US

f.t: The Paiute Indian Tribe of Utah shares The Paiute Language for Beginners, now in its second edition, which anyone can view and download.
In 2003 the Kaibab Band of Paiute Indians and the National Park Service completed a partnership visitor center and museum at Pipe Spring, Arizona.
The Paiute Indian Tribe of Utah Restoration Act of April 3, 1980 brought formal federal recognition to the Cedar Band of Paiute Indians.

n.l: Southern Utah and northern Arizona, US, including Cedar City, Utah, and the Kaibab reservation near Fredonia, Arizona

f.t: Southern Ute government is based on a constitution adopted in 1936 and revised in 1975.
The Tribe's Brunot Area guide explains the hunting right reserved in the 1873 agreement, despite the loss of reservation lands.
The Southern Ute Indian Tribe is made up of the Mouache and Caputa bands and is headquartered in Ignacio, Colorado.
An elected Tribal Council governs the Southern Ute Indian Tribe, which maintains its own constitution, laws and tribal courts.

n.l: Southern Ute Reservation around Ignacio, southwestern Colorado, United States

f.t: Tiwa is the native language of Taos Pueblo, and English and Spanish are also spoken there.
Taos Pueblo, with its multistory adobe homes, gained World Heritage status in 1992 as one of the world's most significant cultural landmarks.
In 1970 a federal law returned 48,000 acres, including Blue Lake, to Taos Pueblo, a landmark for tribal self-determination across the United States.

n.l: Taos valley, northern New Mexico, US

f.t: O’odham groups still speak the O’odham language, part of the Uto-Aztecan family, with dialects that vary from group to group.
The Tohono O’odham Nation has about 28,000 members and a land base of about 2.8 million acres in the Sonoran Desert, roughly the size of Connecticut.

f.p: Sistema de Información Cultural, Secretaría de Cultura (Mexico)
f.t: Divided by the border since the 1850s, O’odham communities in Sonora, Mexico, and Arizona still share a common culture and sense of being one people.

n.l: Sonoran Desert of southern Arizona, US (Sells is the capital), with O’odham communities across the border in Sonora, Mexico

f.t: In 2010, land for the Tonto Apache Tribe was acquired in trust following a land exchange with the U.S. Forest Service.
In 1875, Tonto and Yavapai people were forcibly moved from the Rio Verde Reserve to San Carlos. Some Tonto families later returned to Payson.
The Tonto Apache Tribe is based beside Payson in northwestern Gila County, Arizona.

n.l: Payson, Gila County, Arizona, United States

a: Ute Indian Tribe of the Uintah and Ouray Reservation

f.t: In an April 2026 statement, the Ute Indian Tribe announced it would appeal a federal district court decision concerning split-estate reservation lands.

f.p: Utah Division of State History, History to Go
f.t: In 1881, the United States forcibly removed White River Utes from Colorado to the Uintah Reservation.
The Ute Indian Tribe elects Business Committee representatives from the Uintah, Uncompahgre and Whiteriver bands.
The Tribe delegates protection, restoration and management of Uintah and Ouray Reservation water resources to its Water Resources Department and Commission.

n.l: Uintah and Ouray Reservation, northeastern Utah, with tribal government at Fort Duchesne, United States

f.t: The Weenuche Band organized a tribal government and adopted a constitution six years after the Indian Reorganization Act of 1934.
The Ute Mountain Ute Tribe identifies itself as the Weenuche band of the Ute Nation, with its tribal offices in Towaoc, Colorado.
White Mesa Administration supports community members with employment, education and access to basic services in White Mesa, Utah.
The Ute Mountain Ute Tribal Council is elected by the tribal membership and governs the reservation.

n.l: Towaoc and reservation lands in southwestern Colorado and northwestern New Mexico; White Mesa, Utah, United States

f.p: Sistema de Información Cultural, Secretaría de Cultura (Mexico)
f.t: Warihó and Macurawe families weave baskets, mats and hats from palm and fiber and build harps, violins and guitars. Their craft work is family based and rests with women.

f.p: Sistema de Información Cultural, Secretaría de Cultura (Mexico)
f.t: In colonial times the people formed two branches, one in Chihuahua influenced by the Rarámuri and one in Sonora influenced by the Yoreme.

f.p: Sistema de Información Cultural, Secretaría de Cultura (Mexico)
f.t: The people call themselves Macurawe in Sonora and Warihó in Chihuahua. Their Uto-Aztecan language has two variants and bridges Tarahumara and Mayo.

n.l: Foothills of the Sierra Madre Occidental on the Chihuahua and Sonora border, Mexico

f.t: The White Mountain Apache Tribe has over 12,000 members living in nine major reservation communities, with Whiteriver as its capital.
The White Mountain Apache own and run Sunrise, one of the largest ski resorts in the Southwest, and rare Apache trout swim in reservation streams.
White Mountain Apache people live on 1.6 million acres of their ancestral homeland, the Fort Apache Indian Reservation, set aside in 1891.

n.l: White Mountains of east-central Arizona, US (Fort Apache Indian Reservation, Whiteriver)

f.p: Instituto Nacional de Antropología e Historia (INAH)
f.t: In July 2025 UNESCO added the Wixárika Route through sacred sites to Wirikuta, a 500 km corridor, to the World Heritage List after decades of Wixaritari requests.

f.p: Sistema de Información Cultural, Secretaría de Cultura (Mexico)
f.t: Wixárika artists are known for yarn paintings, made by pressing yarn into a wax base on wooden boards, and for finely worked beadwork.

f.p: Sistema de Información Cultural, Secretaría de Cultura (Mexico)
f.t: At the end of the 1700s Wixárika communities received land titles that defined the boundaries of their present-day communities.

n.l: Sierra Madre Occidental in Jalisco and Nayarit, Mexico, with communities in Durango and Zacatecas

f.t: In September 2026 the Fort McDowell Yavapai Nation, about 950 members, marked 123 years since its land was set aside in 1903.
In 1976 Fort McDowell Yavapai community members voted 144 to 57 against selling their land for the Orme Dam, and in 1981 the dam was called off.
Yavapai people are known for exceptional baskets, and the Yavapai-Prescott Indian Tribe flag carries a historic basket design.

n.l: Central and western Arizona, US, including Fort McDowell near Phoenix and Prescott

f.t: Most Yoeme people today live in the Mexican states of Sonora and Sinaloa, and the federally recognized Pascua Yaqui Tribe is based in Tucson, Arizona.
The Pascua Yaqui Tribe in Arizona gained United States federal recognition on September 18, 1978.

f.p: Sistema de Información Cultural, Secretaría de Cultura (Mexico)
f.t: In 1937 agreements with President Lázaro Cárdenas confirmed Yaqui possession of 485,235 hectares in Sonora as their exclusive territory.

n.l: Yaqui River valley in Sonora, Mexico, and Pascua Yaqui communities near Tucson, Arizona, US

f.t: Yoreme communities have traditional governors. In December 2025 they met Mexico’s federal agrarian office to set a path for continuing the Yoreme-Mayo Justice Plan.

f.p: Sistema de Información Cultural, Secretaría de Cultura (Mexico)
f.t: Yoreme patron saint fiestas strengthen the social networks that link communities across Mayo lands and keep Yoreme identity alive.

f.p: Sistema de Información Cultural, Secretaría de Cultura (Mexico)
f.t: Yoreme artisans make wool blankets and sashes, clay pots, reed mats, harps, violins, rattles and wooden benches with hide seats.

n.l: Southern Sonora (Etchojoa, Huatabampo, Navojoa) and northern Sinaloa (Ahome, El Fuerte, Guasave), Mexico
